articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to offer suggestions for how to reduce Piedmont’s risk from wildfires, earthquakes, and other natural hazards from now through Sunday, March 23. Community members can share their input at piedmont.ca.gov/MitigationStrategy. Community input will be used to inform the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, a FEMA-required document that studies the specific ways Piedmont could be impacted by natural hazards and creates a roadmap for preventative measures the City can take. • Mitigation actions could include: • Updating or adopting new policies, like strengthening building codes • Infrastructure projects like retrofitting or rebuilding critical facilities • Developing programs to help residents make their properties more resilient Residents may submit as many ideas as they wish and will be able to see suggestions that others have submitted. State and federal grant funding Work to update the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan began last fall, with a deep dive into the natural hazards most likely to threaten Piedmont. The project team has worked to document the specific ways each of these hazards could affect Piedmont if they were to occur, including damage to people and property, critical facilities and infrastructure, and the local economy. This work provides context for the project’s current phase – the development of a mitigation strategy. Effective mitigation – actions taken before a disaster that aim to reduce risk – can reduce damage, minimize disruption, and speed recovery from disasters when they happen. When the mitigation plan is complete, the City will submit it to FEMA and the California Office of Emergency Services for review. Receiving approval from these two agencies positions Piedmont to apply for state and federal grants to fund mitigation projects documented in the plan. Residents can learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the 2019 plan at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMP, or subscribe to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews.
articles.title: City seeks suggestions for Hazard Mitigation Plan

articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission heard an update at their March 5 meeting on the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which is currently undergoing a re-evaluation process to ensure the City’s resilience in the face of disaster as well as secure state and federal funding. Delivered by Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, the update provided a primer for the conversations the City will be having in the next months about wildfire prevention, risk of natural disasters, and possible changes to the City’s fire code. A Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) is a FEMA required plan in order to receive mitigation funding. The LHMP update seeks to better prepare Piedmont for natural hazards, including evacuation infrastructure, updates to building codes, and attention on critical facilities in the event of disaster. The plan includes a 5-year roadmap of what the City can do to reduce the impact of natural hazards in Piedmont, providing a “North Star” for resiliency efforts in Piedmont. The plan seeks to prepare the City not just for earthquakes and wildfires, but also less obvious disasters such as landslides and flooding. An upcoming conversation for the City will be this year’s fire code update, raising questions of building code modifications, vegetation management requirements and the code enforcement. “Right now, we primarily enforce via education,” said Brannigan. “We talk with homeowners, we respond to requests to come look at properties. Nancy, Nick and I walk the parks and our open spaces to talk about how we can do fuel reduction and fuel mitigation. We get good compliance that way in Piedmont.” Another measure to reduce fire risk could lie in creating fire-resistant landscaping demonstrations in Piedmont’s public spaces. A dry landscape demonstration garden like this could have the potential to show what a beautiful fire-safe area can look like. The presentation ended with a call to action by Chief Brannigan, encouraging residents to get involved in the process by submitting suggestions online at piedmont.ca.gov/mitigationstrategy and subscribing to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews. In addition, the City will host a Mitigation Strategy Workshop on Wednesday, March 26, from 5:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Brannigan encouraged community members to attend and share feedback on possible mitigation actions.
articles.title: Park Commission hears update on Hazard Mitigation Plan

Community input will be used to inform the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, a FEMA-required document that studies the specific ways Piedmont could be impacted by natural hazards and creates a roadmap for preventative measures the City can take. • Mitigation actions could include: • Updating or adopting new policies, like strengthening building codes • Infrastructure projects like retrofitting or rebuilding critical facilities • Developing programs to help residents make their properties more resilient Residents may submit as many ideas as they wish and will be able to see suggestions that others have submitted. State and federal grant funding Work to update the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan began last fall, with a deep dive into the natural hazards most likely to threaten Piedmont. The project team has worked to document the specific ways each of these hazards could affect Piedmont if they were to occur, including damage to people and property, critical facilities and infrastructure, and the local economy. This work provides context for the project’s current phase – the development of a mitigation strategy. Effective mitigation – actions taken before a disaster that aim to reduce risk – can reduce damage, minimize disruption, and speed recovery from disasters when they happen. When the mitigation plan is complete, the City will submit it to FEMA and the California Office of Emergency Services for review. Receiving approval from these two agencies positions Piedmont to apply for state and federal grants to fund mitigation projects documented in the plan. Residents can learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the 2019 plan at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMP, or subscribe to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews. Park Commission hears update on Hazard Mitigation Plan By Tony Simons The Piedmont Park Commission heard an update at their March 5 meeting on the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which is currently undergoing a re-evaluation process to ensure the City’s resilience in the face of disaster as well as secure state and federal funding. Delivered by Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, the update provided a primer for the conversations the City will be having in the next months about wildfire prevention, risk of natural disasters, and possible changes to the City’s fire code. A Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) is a FEMA required plan in order to receive mitigation funding. The LHMP update seeks to better prepare Piedmont for natural hazards, including evacuation infrastructure, updates to building codes, and attention on critical facilities in the event of disaster. The plan includes a 5-year roadmap of what the City can do to reduce the impact of natural hazards in Piedmont, providing a “North Star” for resiliency efforts in Piedmont. The plan seeks to prepare the City not just for earthquakes and wildfires, but also less obvious disasters such as landslides and flooding. An upcoming conversation for the City will be this year’s fire code update, raising questions of building code modifications, vegetation management requirements and the code enforcement. “Right now, we primarily enforce via education,” said Brannigan. “We talk with homeowners, we respond to requests to come look at properties. Nancy, Nick and I walk the parks and our open spaces to talk about how we can do fuel reduction and fuel mitigation. We get good compliance that way in Piedmont.” Another measure to reduce fire risk could lie in creating fire-resistant landscaping demonstrations in Piedmont’s public spaces. A dry landscape demonstration garden like this could have the potential to show what a beautiful fire-safe area can look like. The presentation ended with a call to action by Chief Brannigan, encouraging residents to get involved in the process by submitting suggestions online at piedmont.ca.gov/mitigationstrategy and subscribing to email updates at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMPnews. articles.text: A creative approach to motivation Sometimes “doing nothing” can be a superpower. We’ve all been there. You plan a fun activity, offer up some great ideas, or even suggest something as simple as going outside, and your kids respond with a solid NO. Or worse—an uninterested shrug. It can be frustrating, especially when you feel like they should be doing something productive, active, or at least engaged with the world around them. But here’s the thing: Sometimes, refusing to do anything is a signal that they need a different kind of approach—or even a little space to be still. So what do you do? Push them? Leave them be? Here’s a creative way to navigate these moments. Reframe “Doing Nothing” as a superpower Instead of panicking that your child is wasting time, consider that rest and boredom are actually important. Boredom fuels creativity, and downtime is essential for mental health. Try shifting your perspective: • If they’re lying on the couch staring at the ceiling, say, “Looks like you’re deep in thought! What big ideas are you working on?” • If they reject all activity suggestions, respond with, “Ahh, the fine art of doing absolutely nothing–you have to practice for that level of skill!” Sometimes, the pressure to be constantly doing can make kids resist even more. A little humor and permission to relax can go a long way. Give them the right kind of choices Instead of asking “Do you want to do something?” (which is easy to say no to), reframe the question: • “Would you rather do something inside or outside?” • “Do you want to pick the activity, or should I surprise you?” • “Should we do something active or something creative?” This small shift puts them in control but still nudges them toward action. articles.text: Thirty-two members of Highlander Robotics attended the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Regional meet in Orange County the weekend of March 1. With their new robot Kelpie they won the Engineering Inspiration Award, and earned their fourth consecutive qualification to the World Championship to be held this April in Houston. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot is built for each season and competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. Teams can win awards based on the performance of their robots; the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs; and the impact they make on their communities. The Highlanders, in the first tournament of the season, arrived as the favorite in a field of 47 teams. After the first day of competition they had a 6-1 record, had set the high score of 170, and were ranked 1st. They lost their final two matches, however, and finished qualifications in third place with a 7-3 record. In the playoff draft, they were first pick of the tournament, selected by the top-seeded Patribots from San Diego. Their three-team alliance was completed by the Firebots from Sunnyvale. In the first round of the double elimination playoffs the Highlanders’ first seeded alliance notched an easy win, 159-64, against the 8th seed captained by Kelpie climbs hanging steel cages in the final moments of a match. Highlander Robotic’s Kelpie qualified for this year’s World Championship Sage Hill Robotics from Newport Coast. In their second round against the 4th seed alliance captained by Dana Point’s Robot Dolphins from Outer Space, the team exited the 15 second autonomous period ahead 51-44. Over the next 2 minutes and 15 seconds however, the Patribots struggled to cope with the opposition’s defense and the alliance lost 141- 164. In the lower bracket, the Highlanders’ alliance adjusted their tactics and the Firebots worked to protect the Patribots from defensive maneuvers. While counter-defense proved ineffective, they still managed to scrape out a 145-115 win and eliminate the 6th seed alliance. In the quarter finals their luck ran out and they lost 151-147 to Atascadero’s Greybots and their 5th seed alliance, finishing 4th overall. In judged awards the Highlanders won FIRST’s Engineering Inspiration award, earning a spot at the World Championship, which celebrates outstanding success in advancing respect and appreciation for engineering within a team’s organization and community. The judges specifically cited their work mentoring middle and elementary school robotics teams, the curriculum they have developed to enable girlscouts to earn robotics badges, the team’s own training systems, and this year’s creation of a full-sized practice field that has been used by 16 other FRC teams. Kelpie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Max Seiden and supported by drive coach Cassie Colby, technician Caetano de Figueiredo, and human player Justin Green. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is composed of 55 students from 17 high schools around the area. They work from the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information visit the team on the web at frc8033.com. This year’s robot, Kelpie, is able to pick up and score 16” kick balls and 4” diameter PVC pipes on a branched steel element called a “reef”. articles.text: PHS dominates Williams 4-1 to win D5 CIF NorCal title Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team is a champion again, this time winning the CIF State NorCal Division 5 championship. Seeded No. 5, they added another title to the trophy cabinet on Saturday, March 8 at Witter Field, dominating No. 7 Williams 4-1 to claim the school’s first CIF State NorCal title. Two days earlier, they beat No. 8 Colusa 2-nil in the semifinals. “We did our research and had the video analysis before the game. articles.text: Highlanders beat Oakland Tech, San Joaquin Memorial Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball season came to an end in the Div.1 CIF State Regional Semifinals. Their two wins at State marks the program’s most since 2015. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball season came to an end on Saturday, March 8 at No. 4 St. Mary’s of Stockton, losing 61-48.Piedmon t was the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State tournament. In earlier rounds, the Highlanders defeated No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial in a heated 62-60 Round II victory at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, March 6, and opened the tournament with a dominant 60-29 win over Oakland Tech on Tuesday, March 4. Against St. Mary’s, Piedmont trailed by just four points at halftime down 35-31, but were limited to just six points in the third quarter. Two days earlier against San Joaquin Memorial, Piedmont battled with the Panthers for all four quarters. PHS took a 35-33 lead at the end of the second quarter and never relinquished from there. In the opening round against Oakland Tech, the Highlanders dominated from the get-go, allowing just one point in the first quarter to lead 14-1 and carried a commanding 34-8 lead by halftime. The regional semifinals mark the farthest Piedmont has gone in the CIF State tournament since 2023.competing in the Open Division, the top flight, Piedmont only played one game in State after receiving the No. 1 seed in the Open Division and a first-round bye. This year’s team advanced the farthest since 2015 when it reached the Regional Finals. “The girls played really hard on both sides,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We’ve had big plays from everyone. We went this far in the Open two years ago, but this is a little bit deeper than we’ve gone in the other brackets in recent years,” “I’m just really humbled and grateful. We just worked together really well and had great chemistry. We came together and had a lot of fun,” said freshman Andrea Martin. Their Round II win required a big-game performance by freshman guard Jenelle Solis, who scored 20 points and had eight assists. “Our mentality was just to win. Andrea Martin had 12 points and nine rebounds against St. Mary’s, 22 points and 10 rebounds on Memorial, and 11 points and 11 boards on Oakland Tech.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team is back at it for the spring 2025 season. So far this season, they defeated Bentley School with a 7-0 shutout at the Corey Reich Tennis Center to start the season on Tuesday, March 4. They also went 2-2 at this year’s California Tennis Classic in Fresno on Friday and Saturday, March 7-8. “We lost a lot of good players. But we’re still pretty good. We did pretty well in Fresno and were placed in the second strongest division. It gave us a chance to see our guys play more,” coach Jim Landes said. Piedmont faced some big departures with the Class of 2024, including singles starters Ben Breber and Arun Brahma, along with doubles champion Monte Imburg. Lucas Smolko seems poised for a big junior year at the No. 1 singles spot for a third consecutive year. He was last year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles champion and reached the D2 NCS Individual Tournament’s singles semifinals against University’s eventual-champion Karam Dhawan. “Lucas has been too strong for all of his opponents; he won all four matches in Fresno. He’s playing well,” Landes said. Nate Welch is another junior who looks poised to back up Smolko in the singles order. Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is gearing up for the spring season with a family-friendly garden tour on Sunday, March 23. “Explore Together” is a family-friendly program designed by garden staff to help visitors of all ages discover the beauty of the Ruth Bancroft Garden while enjoying quality time together outdoors. Visitors can choose to embark on a self-guided tour by grabbing a brochure at the entrance gate or by downloading the tour digitally. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Whether you’re visiting with family, friends or by yourself, the “Explore Together” program invites attendees to explore the garden at an individual pace and immerse yourself in its stunning array of arid and drought-resistant plants and landscapes. Visitors of all ages will learn more about California’s native landscape and members of the Ruth Bancroft Garden can enjoy more offerings including borrowing board games or requesting coloring pages and crayons. Children can borrow an “Explorer Backpack” or “Sensory Backpack” from garden staff for free. Backpacks are filled with hands-on, youth-focused activities and tools to better experience the garden’s offerings. Backpacks are available on a first-come, first-served basis. “Explore Together” hours are from 10 am to 12 pm on Sunday, March 23. The garden is open from 9 am to 4 pm, every Wednesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/visit/ to learn more.

articles.text: Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of Californian modernist artist Ruth Asawa, premieres at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art on April 5. Organized by SFMOMA and New York’s Museum of Modern Art, the exhibition will feature over 300 works of art including looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known, as well as sculptures, drawings, prints, paintings and archival material from public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, a director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective spans over six decades of the artist’s celebrated career and highlights how her longtime San Francisco home and garden served as a muse for her artwork and informed her public sculpture commissions and dedication to arts advocacy in the city. In 1968, Asawa founded the Alvarado School Arts Workshop in San Francisco which laid the foundation for an artists-in-residence program that later expanded to 50 schools. The pioneering artists also helped establish arts festivals and a center for the reuse and distribution of arts materials which is still in operation today. The posthumous retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist, among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums, but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” SFMOMA received a $1.5 million grant from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, in support of the Ruth Asawa: Retrospective. The grant is the largest corporate grant for a single exhibition in the museum’s history, highlighting Asawa’s significance in the Bay Area. “We are grateful to Google.org for their generous support of Ruth Asawa: Retrospective,” said Bedford. “This extraordinary funding will enable SFMOMA to enhance its public programs, community partnerships and free access initiatives in celebration of a legendary artist who continues to have an indelible positive impact on San Francisco.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will be on view at SFMOMA from April 5 through September 2. The museum will offer free admission on April 13 celebrating the retrospective. Admission is also free to residents of the nine Bay Area counties on the first Thursday of each month. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415. 357.4000 for more information. Sculptor Ruth Asawa

By Allyson Aleksey Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is gearing up for the spring season with a family-friendly garden tour on Sunday, March 23. “Explore Together” is a family-friendly program designed by garden staff to help visitors of all ages discover the beauty of the Ruth Bancroft Garden while enjoying quality time together outdoors. Visitors can choose to embark on a self-guided tour by grabbing a brochure at the entrance gate or by downloading the tour digitally. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Whether you’re visiting with family, friends or by yourself, the “Explore Together” program invites attendees to explore the garden at an individual pace and immerse yourself in its stunning array of arid and drought-resistant plants and landscapes. Visitors of all ages will learn more about California’s native landscape and members of the Ruth Bancroft Garden can enjoy more offerings including borrowing board games or requesting coloring pages and crayons. Children can borrow an “Explorer Backpack” or “Sensory Backpack” from garden staff for free. Backpacks are filled with hands-on, youth-focused activities and tools to better experience the garden’s offerings. Backpacks are available on a first-come, first-served basis. “Explore Together” hours are from 10 am to 12 pm on Sunday, March 23. The garden is open from 9 am to 4 pm, every Wednesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/visit/ to learn more. articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson Frances Chung and Joseph Walsh in Scarlett’s Frankenstein at San Francisco Ballet. San Francisco Ballet dancers bring Mary Shelley’s classic gothic horror story Frankenstein to life on stage March 20 through 26, closing the company’s 2024- 25 season. Frankenstein, one of San Francisco Ballet’s biggest box office hits, was created as a co-production between The Royal Ballet and San Francisco Ballet in 2016 and 2017. Choreographer Liam Scarlett’s ballet honors Shelley’s narrative but delivers more poetry and scary-monster thrills than the original 19th century novel. Both book and ballet tell a disturbing and tragic tale about the consequences of abandonment and the risks of tampering with human life, centering on titular character Victor Frankenstein and his ghoulish creation. The science-fiction blockbuster features intriguing and innovative choreography, cinematic design, special effects, pyrotechnics, and a haunting original score from Lowell Liebermann. San Francisco Ballet soloist and stager Lauren Strongin said Scarlett’s choreographer allows audiences to see “his deep respect for classical British technique in the footwork and lower body which then allows for freedom in the upper body and port de bras.” “He often spoke of the movement initiating from the back and allowing the arms to react, as if moving through water,” Strongin said. “Liam was a corps dancer in his career, so you will notice the group work is as difficult as the principal work. There are no superfluous movements or ‘filler’ dance sequences for the group, everything is integral to the story.” Strongin added that Scarlett took his inspiration from Shelley’s novel as a jumping-off point and gave more depth to the central characters. “The contrast of the Creature’s birth into painful, primal, awkward contemporary movements quickly transforming into clean technique mirrors the Creature’s rapid learning of language and social mores in the novel,” she said. “For Victor, his dissent into guilt, paranoia, and fear is expressed by increasingly internal movements.” Ricardo Cervera, a ballet master at The Royal Ballet who taught Scarlett’s Frankenstein choreography to San Francisco Ballet dancers, said “theatrical drama” is one of the ballet’s biggest strengths. “At the end of the first act, you can’t wait to see what comes next, and the same thing at the end of the second act,” he says. “Even though you know [the story], you can’t wait to see what [Liam Scarlett] has done with it.” Single tickets to performances may be purchased online at sfballet.org or by calling ticket services at (415) 865-2000, open Monday through Friday, 10am to 4pm. Frankenstein encore performances will be held on select dates between April 26 through May 4.

articles.text: Sasha De Sola and Joseph Caley in Raymonda Raymonda, San Francisco Ballet’s third production of the 2025– 26 season, opened on March 1 at the War Memorial Theatre. It is a rare sight in the ballet world. Originally choreographed by Marius Petipa for the Imperial Russian Ballet to the music of Alexander Glazunov, the full 180-minute Raymonda is seldom performed today due to its length and complexity. Most companies instead present only the third act. Tamara Rojo’s adaptation, marking the ballet’s North American premiere, is thus an ambitious endeavor—one that highlights the company’s technical and artistic prowess while also showcasing Rojo’s skill as a choreographer. It is a bold attempt to reimagine a classical story ballet in a way that resonates with contemporary audiences, reinforcing ballet’s relevance in the modern world. Yet, despite many delightful moments on Raymonda’s opening night, the overall impression was of a performance that pulled at too many threads without weaving them into a satisfying whole. Rojo’s production replaces the original “damsel in distress” narrative—in which the medieval French countess Raymonda is rescued by her crusader fiancé— with a story of female empowerment inspired by wartime nurse Florence Nightingale. Accordingly, the setting shifts from the era of the Crusades to the 1854 Crimean War, where English, Ottoman, and French forces battle the Russian Empire. Instead of supporting the war effort by sewing alongside her female relatives, the young noblewoman Raymonda (principal dancer Sasha De Sola) defies convention, leaving her family’s estate in England to become a nurse on the Crimean front. There, while tending to the wounded, she becomes entangled in a love triangle with her childhood friend, British officer John de Bryan (guest dancer Joseph Caley), and Ottoman prince Abdur Rahman (Fernando Carratalá Coloma). Her fellow nurses—the free-spirited Henriette (Katherine Barkman) and the dutiful Sister Clemence (Jasmine Jimison)—take sides in the affair, each attempting to sway Raymonda’s choices while delivering some of the production’s most scintillating pas de deux and pas de trois. In the end, Raymonda marries John, leaving Abdur heartbroken. Yet, immediately after the wedding, she walks away from both her husband and her admirer, suitcase in hand, her destination unknown. While the adaptation strives to give Raymonda greater agency and modern relevance, the narrative’s shifts don’t always fully coalesce. Some dramatic moments—like her interactions with Abdur and Constance— flare up vividly but fail to sustain their emotional impact, making it difficult for the dancers to fully immerse in the dramatic arc. These demands were fitting for the ballet’s original comPhotos by Lindsay Thomas missioner, the Imperial Russian Ballet of the 19th century. The choreography includes a cascade of hops en pointe, pirouettes, chaîné turns (half-turns performed while traveling across the stage), and double tours en l’air (jumping turns with two full rotations before landing). The stage is filled with dancers, and the scenes run longer than usual. Taking on a ballet of this scale— one in which many dancers were performing for the first time—is no small feat, even for a company of SF Ballet’s renown. The intricate choreography pushed the dancers to their limits, a challenge they largely rose to, despite a few fleeting missteps in Act III. De Sola danced flawlessly, though perhaps at the expense of emotional depth. Abdur-Hernandez had the only plausible character arc—that of a suffering lover—making his performance the most convincing. For a ballet set during wartime, there was surprisingly little war-related action beyond the Act I brawl between allied troops, which serves as Abdur’s introduction, and the intermittent presence of two wounded soldiers in the left corner of the stage. Despite these shortcomings, Raymonda delivered an abundance of visually arresting sequences. articles.text: Alvin Ailey Dancers The Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater returns to UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall next month for its annual campus residency. It will feature four programs over seven performances and the premieres of four new works and two new productions. The nationally-acclaimed dance company, now in its seventh decade, has regularly performed at Zellerbach Hall, appearing on UC Berkeley’s campus more than any other place in the world outside of their home base in New York City. The company’s current season celebrates the life and legacy of Alvin Ailey Artistic Director Emerita Judith Jamison. UC Berkeley’s Cal Performances dedicates the April 2025 Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater residency and Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp to her legacy as well. Jamison choreographed performances that led her to international stardom and danced with the company until 1980 when she left to pursue opportunities on Broadway. She returned four years later as a choreographer with her debut work Divining. After company founder Alvin Ailey’s death in 1989, Jamison stepped into the role of artistic director, where she remained until she retired in 2011. She passed away on November 9, 2024. In addition to a dedication to the late Jamison, April’s program also features the Bay Area premieres of four new works, including Jamar Roberts’ Al-Andalus Blues, Matthew Rushing’s Sacred Songs, Hope Boykin’s Finding Free, and Lar Lubovitch’s Many Angels, as well as new productions of Ronald K. Brown’s Grace (1999) and Elisa Monte’s Treading (1979). Alvin Ailey dancers will close with its time-honored tradition, performing the beloved Revelations (1960), on three of the four programs. showtimes below. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the ticket office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30pm and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5pm. articles.text: Shotgun Players’ season opener is Yasmina Reza’s internationally acclaimed play, Art, translated by Christopher Hampton and directed by the visionary Emilie Whelan. The production will run from March 8 to April 6 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley, promising an unforgettable theatrical experience that is both thought-provoking and hilariously entertaining. Winner of the Tony Award for Best Play (1998) and the Olivier Award for Best Comedy (1997), Art is a sharp, witty exploration of friendship, identity, and the value of art. The story revolves around three longtime friends – Serge, Marc, and Yvan – whose bonds are tested when Serge buys an expensive, all-white painting. “The play begins with a guy who buys a white painting with 3 white lines for $200,000 and wants to show it to his friends,” said Director Emilie Whelan. “He’s in the middle of life: the middle of his career, the middle of his divorce, the middle of parenting his two kids who are in the middle of how they feel about him. In this mid-life moment, he doesn’t buy a red Corvette... he buys a $200,000 painting. How will his closest friends - who are in the dangerous middle of their own lives - respond to his purchase? Can we buy a new start? Can we buy a blank canvas?” What begins as merely a debate over aesthetics quickly spirals into an uproarious examination of personal relationships and the fragility of human connections. Marc ridicules Serge’s purchase, while Yvan tries to mediate, leading to intense debates about art, personal values, and their long-standing friendship. Yasmina Reza is a French

articles.text: Four-time Grammy-winning Rosanne Cash, Johnny Cash’s eldest daughter, is the latest celebrity to support one of Oakland’s hidden gems: on Tuesday, April 1, Cash will play an intimate benefit concert for the Northern Light School, a unique PreK-8th grade independent school dedicated to serving children from all socioeconomic backgrounds. Past star supporters have included Bonnie Raitt, MC Hammer, Jackson Browne, Bob Weir, and the late all-star Vida Blue. The event will be held at the Oakland Zoo and emceed by renowned actor and activist Peter Coyote. Ticket prices range from $1,000-$3,000 and can be purRosanne Cash chased by the general public at tinyurl.com/NLSBenefit. At Northern Light School, 75 percent of students receive tuition assistance compared to the national average for independent schools of less than 25 percent. 95 percent of NLS’s students are children of color, compared to the national average of 34 percent, and nearly all graduates matriculate to private or parochial high schools. Tickets are tax-deductible and support a great cause. Northern Light School (NLS) is an independent progressive school in Oakland, CA serving students in Pre-K to 8th grade. NLS is committed to providing an empowering education for children from all socioeconomic and cultural backgrounds. Our faculty and staff create an atmosphere where every child can excel — as learners, leaders, and engaged human beings. Our focus is on academic excellence as well as non-violence, acceptance of differences, respect for the environment, and the moral advancement of humanity — so that the children develop an understanding that they have a responsibility to make a difference in the lives of others.

articles.text: Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey is a remake of the 1963 Disney film of the same name. It is based on the 1960 Sheila Burnford children’s story about three animals – Shadow (Don Ameche), a wise old Golden Retriever; Chance (Michael J. Fox), a spunky American Bulldog; and Sassy (Sally Field), a pampered Himalayan cat. The genius of Disney has, since its inception, been the ability to give animals, animated or real, human characteristics, from speech and dress, to facial characteristics. It’s referred to as anthropomorphism. Homeward Bound is a live action feature wherein the animals chat each other up, and make a plan to solve what they perceive to be their dilemma. As Disney has long ago learned, kids find giving human voices to animals completely acceptable, even when animation is blended with live action characters. The plot of Homeward Bound revolves around the decision of the Seavers family to relocate to San Francisco. It’s decided that while making the transition to the new digs, they will leave their three pets with a relative who owns a ranch in northern California. Due to a mix-up in communication, the owner leaves on a cattle drive assuming that the trio will be cared for by a friend, Frank (Gary Taylor). He thinks the pets have been taken along on the drive. The result is that Shadow, Chance, and Sassy believe they’ve, in effect, been left home alone. Shadow decides that he is not going to stay at the ranch, but make his way to San Francisco. Chance and Sassy, at first reluctant, agree to go with him on what will be an epic journey into the rocky mountain wilderness of the Sierra Nevada. And so their adventure begins as these three, who are not prepared for what awaits them, set out on their trek. Of course, they will encounter one crisis after another (Shadow and Chance get separated from Sassy, while crossing a swift-moving river). Of course, Sassy survives and is rescued by an old-timer, Quentin (William Edward Phipps), and is later reunited with Chance and Shadow. The three will encounter mountain lions, bears, and a little girl named Molly who is lost in the woods and they help in her rescue. The rescue party that has been looking for Molly, assuming they’re helping, takes the trio to an animal shelter, from which they eventually escape. Once again the three hit the road so to speak, their destination still San Francisco, hopefully to be rejoined with their owners, the Seavers family. Remember, this is Disney, and after a long and exciting ordeal, the story has right ending. Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey. Directed by Duwayne Dunham. With voices of Don Ameche, Michael J. Fox, Sally Field. Walt Disney Pictures 1 hr., 24 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Kiki’s Delivery Service Kiki’s Delivery Service, created by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, who is regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, was adapted from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes with her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, KiKi’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure; however, it is also a personal crossroads for KiKi, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. pages.text: Wednesday, March 12, 2025 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey By Chris Honoré Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey is a remake of the 1963 Disney film of the same name. It is based on the 1960 Sheila Burnford children’s story about three animals – Shadow (Don Ameche), a wise old Golden Retriever; Chance (Michael J. Fox), a spunky American Bulldog; and Sassy (Sally Field), a pampered Himalayan cat. The genius of Disney has, since its inception, been the ability to give animals, animated or real, human characteristics, from speech and dress, to facial characteristics. It’s referred to as anthropomorphism. Homeward Bound is a live action feature wherein the animals chat each other up, and make a plan to solve what they perceive to be their dilemma. As Disney has long ago learned, kids find giving human voices to animals completely acceptable, even when animation is blended with live action characters. The plot of Homeward Bound revolves around the decision of the Seavers family to relocate to San Francisco. It’s decided that while making the transition to the new digs, they will leave their three pets with a relative who owns a ranch in northern California. Due to a mix-up in communication, the owner leaves on a cattle drive assuming that the trio will be cared for by a friend, Frank (Gary Taylor). He thinks the pets have been taken along on the drive. The result is that Shadow, Chance, and Sassy believe they’ve, in effect, been left home alone. Shadow decides that he is not going to stay at the ranch, but make his way to San Francisco. Chance and Sassy, at first reluctant, agree to go with him on what will be an epic journey into the rocky mountain wilderness of the Sierra Nevada. And so their adventure begins as these three, who are not prepared for what awaits them, set out on their trek. Of course, they will encounter one crisis after another (Shadow and Chance get separated from Sassy, while crossing a swift-moving river). Of course, Sassy survives and is rescued by an old-timer, Quentin (William Edward Phipps), and is later reunited with Chance and Shadow. The three will encounter mountain lions, bears, and a little girl named Molly who is lost in the woods and they help in her rescue. The rescue party that has been looking for Molly, assuming they’re helping, takes the trio to an animal shelter, from which they eventually escape. Once again the three hit the road so to speak, their destination still San Francisco, hopefully to be rejoined with their owners, the Seavers family. Remember, this is Disney, and after a long and exciting ordeal, the story has right ending. Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey. Directed by Duwayne Dunham. With voices of Don Ameche, Michael J. Fox, Sally Field. Walt Disney Pictures 1 hr., 24 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. Kiki’s Delivery Service a wonderful film from Japan A scene from Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey A scene from Kiki’s Delivery Service By Chris Honoré Kiki’s Delivery Service, created by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, who is regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, was adapted from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes with her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, KiKi’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure; however, it is also a personal crossroads for KiKi, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met on March 3 at the Community Hall with a record turnout of 26 readers. Participating were Nancy Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Mike Henn, Lois Price, Laura Goldman, Pat McMahon, Nadine Guffanti, Peggy Shultz, Darby Gregg, Melba Yee, Adrienne Hamlin, Bob Hall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Orrel Lanter, Louise Booth, Sarah Johnson, Hilary Honore, Ken Young, June Yee, Carol Warren, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Gerry Gregg, Martin Levy, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. At their meeting the month before the readers tried something new. The group has grown significantly. Some readers wanted a smaller group experience, so they set up in an alcove for their conversation. It was successful, so at this March meeting four readers led by Lois Price did it again, while Priscilla Wanerus continued to lead the larger discussion. Carol Long once again brought cookies that were enjoyed by all. The group was there to talk about James by Percival Everett. It was published in 2024 and won the National Book Award for Fiction last year. The novel is a reimagining of Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, but is told from the perspective of Huck’s friend, Jim, an escaped enslaved person. Readers’ reactions to James were generally positive but varied. They ranged from “loved it” to “liked it, not loved it” to “not disliked it, not loved it.” This should not have been surprising because there are many layers and facets to James. It was felt this is really two books in one. Readers thought the first part of the book was fun and clever, fine for children, but the second is characterized by violence and book. James code-switches and speaks “correct incorrect grammar” to his white tormentors, but uses unlikely, articulate, formal English with other Blacks. Readers recognized the potential for discrimination based on the way people talk. How someone speaks does not reflect their intelligence, and just because someone talks like you, it doesn’t mean the person is like you. Some readers reread Huckleberry Finn for a comparison and saw it as a very different book. It’s “an adventure story of a kid.” They couldn’t see Twain thinking of Jim as James, and his ending was embarrassing for some. Everett’s ambiguous ending for James was unsatisfying for some readers too, but they felt it was probably necessary given James’ uncertain future. The group also asked if Everett’s work would have stood up on its own without Huckleberry Finn. They thought so, but it would be a different book. Everett’s taking of Twain’s classic work and giving it a new perspective was daring. It generated attention and undoubtedly book sales too. After their separate discussions, the two groups rejoin for the selection of their next book. They had previously selected Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz for their April book and Cloudstreet by Tim Winton for May. After Bob Hall’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected How We Got to Now by Stephen Johnson for June. With their business done, the readers went outside the Community Hall for a group picture. The group’s next discussion will be on April 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. Everett’s dark humor may generate an occasional smile, but this is not a humorous story. It presents the South’s “Peculiar Institution” of slavery as a brutal form of repression. It seemed to the group that Everett used the book to channel his anger regarding whites’ mistreatment of Black people. Some readers found his portrayal of the book’s white characters problematic. They are all ignorant and evil. Readers may have to suspend disbelief at times about his story, as realism is not Everett’s game with this book. His message is the game. Everett is a USC English professor, and he wants to forcefully make a point. Black people have been treated very badly in America. They are strong people, who should be respected, and he commands it with James. Readers found the book to be full of imagery. They particularly liked the use of James’ ownership of a pencil to represent the importance of literacy and its power. Enslaved people were not allowed to learn to read or write. articles.text: It’s tax season again — which also means, unfortunately, that it’s time for the annual array of scams aimed at taxpayers. Fortunately, by being alert, you can protect yourself from these attempts to defraud you. Your first line of defense is to recognize the warning signs of potential tax scams. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) cites these common red flags: • Promises of big payments — If you’ve filed taxes for many years, either by yourself or with the help of a tax professional, you probably have a pretty good idea of whether you’re getting a refund, and how much it will be. But scammers, often using social media, may promise huge refunds by essentially encouraging you to claim tax credits to which you’re not entitled and then charging large, upfront fees or a fee based on your refund amount. • Suspicious websites — Watch out for strange-sounding or misspelled web links — these can take you to harmful sites, rather than the official site of the IRS (IRS.gov). • Solicitations from charity imposters — The many natural disasters we’ve experienced in recent years has brought out great support from people wanting to help friends, neighbors and even total strangers. However, these catastrophes have also encouraged scammers who solicit contributions to bogus charitable groups. To determine whether an organization is a qualified charity that can receive tax-deductible contributions, visit the Tax Exempt Organization Search tool on IRS.gov. • Threats or demands — IRS impersonators may threaten you with large fines, or even arrest, if you don’t make immediate payments of what they claim you owe. You can protect yourself from many tax-related scams by knowing how the IRS will or won’t communicate with you. Typically, the IRS will initiate contact with you through regular mail delivered by the U.S. Postal Service. You can verify the legitimacy of any letter by visiting your secure IRS online account, under the “Notices and Letters” section. Other ways the IRS will contact you: • Email — Only with your permission, with a few exceptions, such as criminal investigations • Text – Only with your permission • Phone — Only to discuss your case, verify information or set up a meeting • Fax — Only to verify or request employment information • In-person visit — Rarely done, and typically only following a letter The IRS will not: • Contact you or take payment on social media. • Accept gift cards or prepaid debit cards as payment. • Threaten to call law enforcement or immigration officials. • Take your citizenship status, driver’s license or business license. • Leave pre-recorded voicemails (robocalls). • Mail tax debt resolution advertisements. If you have doubts about any offers or communications, whether supposedly from the IRS or not, you may want to contact a trusted, qualified tax professional. Also, be on guard for your elderly family members, as senior citizens are frequent targets of scammers. If you talk to these family members regularly, see if you can find out about any unusual offers or solicitations they may have received. Finally, if you believe you are a victim of monetary or identity theft, you can report these issues using the IRS website at IdentityTheft.gov. You can also refer to IRS Publication 5027 — l Identity Theft Information for Taxpayers. Tax scams and identity theft are serious threats — so do whatever you can to defend yourself. articles.text: All of the different housing types we use can be divided into two main categories: single-family housing, and multi-family housing. While the vast majority of people in the industrialized urban world live in multi-family housing of one kind or another, in the U.S. an estimated 80% of housing units are single family, and 20-25% as multi family. There are a number of variations and hybrids, along with varying labels for the different types of housing but in my experience, the types shown in the accompanying diagram are common and understood by architects, developers, contractors and planners. For all communities the end result of different housing types is different densities, typically measured in units/acre. There is a huge difference from say, 3.5 units/acre for single family detached homes, to 12 units/acre for attached townhomes, to as many as 90 units/acre for urban high-rise multi-family. There are also many interconnected components to housing density and the resulting look, feel, and functioning of a neighborhood, including open space, roadway size and type, public transportation systems, and infrastructures of various kinds. (And parking, which we will leave for another column.) In my mind, a dividing line in the whole multi-family world can be defined by the entries. Units with their own separate outside entries, such as duplexes, townhouses or garden apartments, have a whole different character than denser types such as mid or high-rise buildings with entries necessarily located off a common corridor. The units in these denser, higher buildings can’t have the individuality, residential character and connection to the street that the lower density units do. The description of different architectural types of housing is sometimes confused with ownership categories. For example, a 10-unit “apartment” building can be owned by one person, in which case the 10 units would be rented out. This is the most common definition of “apartment”. But the same 10-unit building could also be a condominium, in which case the 10 occupants would each own the inside of their own unit with everything else being considered common space owned jointly by the 10 owners. In this case it would typically be called a “condo” and not an apartment building. Other forms of ownership such as co-ops are somewhat similar. In any case, these different types of ownership can be applied to all of the different architectural types, not just multi-family. Special purpose multi-family housing. like student housing, senior housing, affordable housing, or low-income housing, also can be designed in many of the architectural types, under a variety of ownership formulas, with the one-owner “apartment” model probably most common. Next: Multi-family Housing, Part 2 Will Adams was a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on August 18, 2021. Outside of central zones, like downtown Oakland or the Lake Merritt area, we are most familiar with single family detached (SFD) housing. Some “attached” single family units can be 4 times as dense as single-family dwellings, although still technically considered single family.

He was also a Wednesday walker and led many walks for the group devoted to the different styles of architecture in Piedmont. Last Wednesday, walker and fellow architect Jim Kellogg led a tour of Julia Morgan designed homes, like the first walk Will led for the group in 2021. Jim began the tour with a remembrance of Will’s 2021 walk with information about Julia Morgan and the homes she designed. Morgan’s family moved to the Bay Area from New York when she was two years old, and she spent the rest of her life here. She graduated from the University of California, Berkeley in 1894 with a degree in Civil Engineering. It did not have a School of Architecture then, so Morgan applied and became the first woman admitted to the architecture program at L’Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris and then became the first woman architect licensed in California. Morgan formed her own firm in 1904, after studying with Bernard Maybeck and working for two years with John Galen Howard. She was a constant worker completely dedicated to her profession and never married. She was also an excellent manager and developed a special rapport with craftsmen and artisans working on her projects and managed a hundred people at the peak of her Hearst Castle project. She designed over 700 other California projects including the Berkeley Greek Theater, the Berkeley City Club, the Mills College Campanile, the Carnegie Library, the Monterey Asilomar Conference Center, Piedmont Avenue’s Chapel of the Chimes, Piedmont’s Ransom Bridges School on Hazel Lane, and many others. She was known for delivering projects on time and on budget. Morgan embraced the Arts and Crafts Movement supported by Bernard Maybeck in her architectural work. She strove to reconcile her exposure and training in other styles including BeauxArts formalism, Classical, and Neo-Tudor, while at the same time adding artistry and whimsy to her designs. She was also an excellent engineer pioneering the aesthetic use of reinforced structural concrete as well as inventive custom cement mixes for decorative sculpture and detailing. Morgan designed about 10 beautiful homes that remain in Piedmont. They were all designed within a period of 15 years after Piedmont’s founding in 1907, a time when the city was referred to as “Queen of The Hills” and the “The City of Millionaires.” Her design style and masterpiece projects added to the accuracy of these monikers, as well as the character of Piedmont that we still enjoy today. Jim’s tour would also touch on work by Morgan’s fellow architects of this period. They significantly influenced each other. After providing this background, Jim led the long parade of walkers to see eight of Morgan’s projects. They went up Sierra Avenue for the first two. Several Sierra homes represent the varying architectural styles in the early era of Piedmont’s development and influenced Morgan’s work. They included an arts and crafts home by John Hudson Thomas at 12 Sierra, an elegant beaux-arts classical revival across the street, and a neo-tutor manor house with steep double gable roofs. The first Morgan home was a simple yet beautiful steep-roofed neo-tutor at 49 Sierra built in 1914. It provided an interesting contrast to her house next door at 45 Sierra that was designed in 1925. It represents her mature craftsman’s style with handcrafted detailing. Morgan’s site plan included an elegant, shared porte-cochere driveway and rear yard garage to unify the two homes. The group continued up Lakeview Avenue to Sea View Avenue and stopped at 25 Sea View, an elegantly proportioned classical revival with a Parisian cantilevered glass entry overhang built in 1915. This is not a Morgan house but is an excellent example of Beaux-Arts style that was ingrained in her early education. The walkers continued on Sea View to Hampton Avenue to see. one of Morgan’s masterpieces at 216 Hampton that was built in 1912. The owner agreed to have the group into the yard and go around the house to study the elegant arts and crafts detailing. The house has had only two owners, and they have retained its original layout and character for over 100 years. The beautiful, mature landscaping surrounding the property made the walkers feel they had left modern Piedmont and entered a 1920s “quiet secret garden.” A large turnout of 59 walkers and five K-9 best friends was at the Exedra last Wednesday for a walk by the Walking on Wednesdays group in memory of Will Adams, who died unexpectedly in December.
